summary: A millimetre-scale crust consortium grows over stable cooled volcanic rock, combining a green photosynthetic layer, mineral-weathering partners and the ancestral nitrogen fixer. Hydrated oxygen-protected cells permit intermittent nitrogen input; dust and dead tissue gradually accumulate around colony margins. Red-purple screening strengthens with sustained exposure, especially on high slopes, while sheltered colonies remain greener (F7, F9, F14, F24, F25).

chains.trait: Mineral-weathering crust with oxygen-protected nitrogen-fixing cells
links: Exposed cooled lava and erosion surfaces provide mineral substrate but little accumulated organic matter or available nitrogen.
Photosynthetic partners supply carbon, while microbial acids slowly weather accessible mineral surfaces and may mobilize mineral-bound phosphorus.
The ancestral nitrogen fixer operates in specialized cells with restricted oxygen entry and respiratory oxygen consumption when hydration and energy supply permit.
Drying or excessive oxygen exposure suspends fixation without necessarily killing the symbiont.
Crust texture traps dust, and turnover adds organic matter to small rooting pockets; phosphorus and water can still limit development.
chains.play: Find dust-filled margins where later pioneers can establish; compare hydrated active crust with dry surviving patches and nearby bare rock.
chains.weakness: Colonization requires suitable moisture and stable cooled rock. Nitrogen fixation stops during drying or failed oxygen protection; phosphorus shortage, local acidification, abrasion, trampling and burial interrupt development.
observe: Fine dust remains lodged along raised crust margins after wind clears nearby rock.
A naturally lifted edge exposes a thin green layer that swells after wetting, without making nitrogen fixation directly visible.
Small grass seedlings occur in accumulated debris beside older crust patches.

plausibility.judge: strict review: sol (codex) + DeepSeek; chair sol
plausibility.summary: Acids weather mineral surfaces gradually; the crust does not rapidly split intact basalt. Nitrogen fixation does not remove phosphorus or water limitation, and succession has no universal timetable. Strict review (2026-11-19): revised: Unspecified protected microsites did not explain nitrogenase survival in oxygen-rich air, so the rewrite supplies specialized oxygen protection and separates symbiont survival from active fixation. Residual: F7 and F9 support exposed volcanic substrates, and F24 supplies an ancestral nitrogen-fixing symbiont. Restricted oxygen entry plus respiratory consumption directly addresses F5's elevated oxygen. Slow weathering, conditional phosphorus mobilization and dust retention form a defensible succession mechanism. Residual weakness: oxygen protection consumes carbon and must remain effective during hydration; neither F24 nor nitrogen availability guarantees a positive nutrient balance.

analogues.mechanism: Mineral-weathering associations illustrate gradual substrate alteration, while specialized nitrogen-fixing cells illustrate oxygen protection; active fixation still requires hydration, energy and sufficient nutrients.

chains.trait: Exposure-responsive red-purple screening above a green photosynthetic layer
links: Exposed colonies receive more radiation than adjacent shaded fissures, and high slopes receive elevated UV, reaching approximately 1.4 times Earth's at 2,000 m.
Excess UV and visible irradiance can damage the photosynthetic layer even where planetary UV is below Earth's reference value.
A superficial red-purple layer with suitable UV and blue-light absorption reduces damaging radiation reaching living cells.
Screening strengthens under sustained exposure but costs carbon, can reduce useful light and can increase heating.
chains.play: Read local exposure differences from neighbouring red and green colonies; high-slope screening is common, but colour is neither an elevation meter nor an alkaloid test.
chains.weakness: Screening does not prevent overheating or dehydration; heavy screening reduces performance in deep shade, and visible redness alone does not measure UV protection.
observe: Exposed high-slope colonies show stronger red-purple screening than nearby shaded fissures.
A chipped natural edge shows green beneath the coloured surface.
Hot dry colonies look shrunken despite retaining their red screen.

plausibility.judge: strict review: sol (codex) + DeepSeek; chair sol
plausibility.summary: The overlay follows the seeded pigment canon. Earth lichen screens support the mechanism, not an exact pigment identity. Red here signals exposure stress; it does not imply alkaloids or a crater-wide metal anomaly. Strict review (2026-11-19): revised: The rewrite distinguishes altitude-related UV, local irradiance and heating while making pigment absorption explicit without imposing an unsupported Earth-relative damage threshold. Residual: F14 explicitly supplies the altitude-dependent UV exposure, and F25 supplies red-purple overlays over ancestral green pigmentation. The chain appropriately requires suitable absorption rather than assuming redness proves UV screening. Residual weakness: pigment identity and absorption spectrum remain fictional, and pigmentation integrates exposure history rather than reporting current irradiance.

analogues.mechanism: Cortical pigments illustrate screening of underlying photosynthetic cells only; they do not establish this consortium's structure or exact pigment chemistry.

gameplay.notes: Babosa consumes softened dead margins and associated decaying material. Uniform red-purple screening lacks the red-veined alkaloid pattern and indicates exposure stress rather than toxicity. Arsenic or mercury contamination near geothermal seeps remains a separate hazard without a dependable pigment warning (F23). This is a soil-building community rather than a concentrated edible mineral deposit. Crater-rim occupancy indicates suitable rock, not the second capsule's purpose. The common name refers to an ash-like appearance, not a requirement for fresh ash.

relations.note: Creates dust-and-litter microsites beside fissures where the grass may establish; mature grass can later shade the crust.
Shares cooled lava terrain where damp nutrient-poor seeps interrupt otherwise dry surfaces.
Consumes softened dead margins and associated decaying material on damp ground.
Can occupy exposed rock beside crater vegetation; adjacency establishes no shared metal specialization.

generator.trunk: None; a tightly attached crust follows the rock surface.

branching.buttress: None; structural branching parameters are inactive.

leaf.arrangement: Contiguous irregular plates with expanding colony margins

overlay_rules: Red-purple screening responds to sustained local exposure and becomes more prevalent on exposed high slopes.
Lowland colonies usually remain greener; shaded fissures reduce screening at any altitude.
Naturally exposed inner tissue remains greener.
Dust occupies cracks rather than replacing the living pigment.
Do not use a fixed altitude cutoff or redness as a toxin detector.

placement.slope: Stable rock faces, 0–70 degrees; favour moisture-retaining texture.
placement.wetness: Intermittently damp with drying intervals; not permanently submerged.
placement.soil: Cooled basalt and cohesive tuff with little developed soil; exclude hot active vent surfaces.
placement.fog: Fog wetting favours activity where droplets reach the surface.
placement.density: Discontinuous colonies on suitable bare rock, merging locally where stability and wetting persist; no universal succession timetable.
substrate_contexts: Basalt lava fields include surfaces from the eruption approximately 400 years ago or older; erosion can expose fresh bare surfaces without a new eruption (F7, F9).
The approximately 12,000-year-old crater rim is cohesive tuff; generate crust only on presently exposed stable rock, independently of time since impact (F22).

generator.seasonal: Growth and nitrogen fixation follow suitable hydration; drying suspends fixation and metabolic activity. Alpine patches remain inactive beneath persistent snow.
generator.wind_response: The adherent crust does not sway; airborne grit abrades exposed margins while rough patches retain dust.

journal.en: A red skin on the stone, green underneath. Dust stays where it has taken hold.
journal.es: Una piel roja sobre la piedra, verde por debajo. El polvo se queda donde ha prendido.

observe: The red skin follows every hollow in the cooled stone.
Green tissue shows at a naturally broken edge.
Dust gathers where a colony meets a damp fissure.
secrets: The best seedling microsites occur where old crust margins meet water-holding cracks, rather than at the reddest colony centres.
Similar crust on ordinary lava and crater-rim rock prevents its colour from serving as a unique meteor clue.
